claim: PM Modi's photoshoot during the election campaign in Kerala.
justification: The viral image depicting PM Modi posing for a professional photoshoot (holding coconuts, surrounded by a film crew) during the Kerala election campaign was investigated by multiple independent fact-checking organizations (CyberPeace, Newschecker, DigitEye, Lighthouse Journalism) and PIB Fact Check, all of which found it to be AI-generated using Gemini, with no real event behind it. While Modi did campaign in Kerala ahead of the April 9, 2026 elections, no actual photoshoot occurred.

claim: The U.S. Navy was created "to free international waters from the Barbary pirates."
justification: Multiple historians consulted by PolitiFact Florida, as well as the U.S. Navy's own historical command, confirm that the permanent U.S. Navy was established via the 1794 Naval Act specifically in response to Barbary pirate attacks on American shipping. PolitiFact rated Donalds' statement 'Mostly True,' noting it is accurate though it omits some nuance in his broader comparison to the Iran situation.

claim: Hezbollah attacked Israeli military headquarters.
justification: Independent fact-checking by CyberPeace Research Wing specifically investigated this claim from Facebook user 'Nazim Khan Tirwadiya' and traced the viral video to a real but unrelated apartment fire in Manhattan, New York City on April 12, 2026, confirming no Hezbollah attack on any Israeli military headquarters occurred as depicted. The footage was verified via reverse image search, matching street imagery, and NYFD's own social media confirming it was a domestic fire incident, not a military strike.

claim: In Kushinagar, Uttar Pradesh, headmaster Naeemuddin raped a five-year-old girl.
justification: While headmaster Naeemuddin Ansari was initially suspected and briefly detained based on rumors and a family member's suspicion, a thorough police investigation found he had no role in the crime and he was released without charge. The actual perpetrator was identified as Surendra Singh, a family acquaintance, who confessed and was arrested under POCSO. Fact-checkers (The Quint) explicitly rated the claim that Naeemuddin committed the rape as 'False'.

claim: Solar and wind have not reached “3% of global energy.”
justification: Independent data (Energy Institute/BP-based analysis, Wikipedia energy breakdowns) and a direct PolitiFact fact-check confirm that wind and solar account for roughly 3% of global primary/total energy consumption, matching Wright's specific figure. However, this metric excludes the much higher 15% share these sources hold in global electricity generation specifically, and fact-checkers noted the framing understates how fast renewables are growing.

claim: “Middle-income countries generally have higher or similar prices compared to Kenya.”
justification: Independent fact-checking found mixed evidence: Tanzania, a nearly identical lower-middle-income peer, actually has slightly lower fuel prices than Kenya despite having roughly half Kenya's GNI per capita, directly undercutting the claim. Morocco, a higher-income comparator, does have slightly higher prices, supporting the claim in that instance. Fact-checkers concluded the claim is misleading because it lumps together economically diverse countries under one label to make Kenya's higher prices seem more typical than the actual data shows.

claim: In Tamil Nadu, Rahul Gandhi praised AIADMK instead of DMK.
justification: Independent fact-checks (Fact Crescendo, Newschecker) found the viral clip used to support this claim was deceptively edited. Rahul Gandhi's full remarks acknowledged AIADMK's historical role but then sharply criticized its current leadership as a 'hollow shell' and 'instrument of the BJP,' while explicitly affirming that DMK and Congress's alliance was defending Tamil interests against the BJP/RSS. Fact-checkers explicitly concluded he did not praise AIADMK 'instead of' DMK.

claim: Order issued by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas increasing petrol and diesel prices by ₹10 and ₹12.50 on 29 April 2026.
justification: The PIB Fact Check unit and the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas explicitly and repeatedly stated that no such order was issued, calling the circulating document fake and fabricated. Multiple independent news outlets (NewsX, Republic World, Zee News, Newschecker, Telangana Today, etc.) corroborate that this was a hoax document mimicking an official order, with fuel prices unchanged since April 2022.

claim: “Oil per barrel in 2022, around May, was around $115 per barrel, but the amount Kenyans paid at the pump, the highest ever they paid, was KSh160 for petrol and KSh140 for diesel.”
justification: Brent crude averaged $113.34/barrel in May 2022, close to the claimed $115. EPRA's own records confirm petrol hit Sh159.12 and diesel Sh140.00 in Nairobi, explicitly described as a record high in Kenya's history at the time. The only imprecision is that this record retail price took effect from mid-June 2022 (based on May's landing costs), not literally 'in May,' which is a minor timing simplification rather than a factual error in the figures themselves.

claim: A newspaper clipping claims that Indira Gandhi appealed to citizens in 1967 to stop buying gold due to a foreign exchange crisis.
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (The Hindu itself, CyberPeace, DFRAC, Fact Crescendo, Newschecker, The Quint) confirm the viral June 6, 1967 front page is digitally altered/AI-generated and does not exist in The Hindu's archives; the real front page that day covered the Arab-Israel war, not a gold appeal. While the Indira Gandhi government did later impose gold restrictions via the 1968 Gold Control Act, there is no evidence of a 1967 public newspaper appeal matching the clipping's specific claim.

claim: “Mifepristone sends 1 in 10 women who use it to the emergency room with life threatening conditions."
justification: Hawley's figure stems from a non-peer-reviewed EPPC report that measured a composite 10.93% 'serious adverse event' rate combining sepsis, infection, hemorrhage, and ER visits—not specifically ER visits for life-threatening conditions. Independent medical experts and organizations like the Society of Family Planning say the study improperly counted routine ER visits (even without confirmed complications) as serious adverse events, and FDA's own postmarketing data shows serious complications occur in under 1% of cases, contradicting the 1-in-10 figure Hawley cites as representing life-threatening ER visits.

claim: In 2020, “Amy Acton called off Ohio’s election at the last minute.”
justification: While Acton did sign the order closing polls the night before Ohio's March 2020 primary, multiple fact-checks and Governor DeWine himself (who appointed her and endorsed Ramaswamy) have stated repeatedly that the decision was his, made jointly with bipartisan state leaders including the Republican Secretary of State and Lt. Governor, and that Acton signed the order at his direction. The claim's framing that Acton unilaterally 'called off' the election omits this crucial context about where authority and decision-making actually resided.

claim: An archive page of 'The Hindu' from 1967 showing Indira Gandhi's appeal not to buy gold.
justification: The viral archive page attributed to The Hindu dated June 6, 1967, showing Indira Gandhi appealing against gold purchases, was confirmed fake by The Hindu itself, its journalists (who shared the authentic front page showing Arab-Israeli war coverage instead), and multiple independent fact-checkers who found forensic inconsistencies (wrong dateline, wrong logo, wrong tagline) indicating AI/digital fabrication. No genuine appeal of this kind by Indira Gandhi in 1967 has been found in any archive.

claim: "As soon as" the war in Iran is over, "you’re going to see gasoline and oil [prices] drop like a rock."
justification: A dedicated finance report explicitly confirms Trump made this exact statement to reporters in the Oval Office on May 11, 2026, when gas averaged $4.52/gallon. This matches his repeated rhetoric throughout the Iran war period, where he used nearly identical phrasing on multiple other dated occasions (April 30, early May, and later in 2026).

claim: “We just approved two new drugs, two new oncology drugs, in record time, one in 45 days. The closest before that was 310 days.”
justification: Kennedy's specific day counts (44/45 and 55 days) are roughly accurate for the post-filing review period, but calling this 'record time' is false since a 1996 HIV drug (Crixivan) was approved faster (42 days), as even Kennedy's own FDA Commissioner acknowledged. More importantly, the comparison to '310 days' is misleading because it pits a narrow post-filing review metric against the full submission-to-approval average; the actual submission-to-approval times for these two drugs were 104 and 90 days, and neither drug was truly 'new' since both were expanded indications or combinations of already-approved drugs.

claim: Dharmendra Pradhan Pictured With NEET Leak Accused
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (The Quint, Fact Crescendo, Newschecker) confirmed via reverse image search that the woman in the viral photo with Dharmendra Pradhan is Nivedita Ekbote, principal of Modern College and BJYM state vice president, not NEET paper leak accused Manisha Mandhare. The photo dates to December 2024, predating the 2026 NEET leak controversy, and Ekbote herself publicly denied the claim as misrepresentation of her identity.

claim: Says his cognitive test results showed he has “extreme intelligence.”
justification: Trump did make this statement on Truth Social in May 2026 after a perfect MoCA score, so the attribution is accurate. However, the substantive claim that this proves 'extreme intelligence' is false: medical experts and the test's creator, Dr. Ziad Nasreddine, confirm the MoCA is a dementia/cognitive-impairment screening tool, not an IQ or intelligence test, and a perfect score only indicates no screening errors, not exceptional intellect.

claim: “And if [Vice President JD Vance] does really great” at finding fraud, “we’ll have a balanced budget without having to do anything."
justification: Multiple independent outlets (Colorado Politics, Fox Business, Washington Examiner, RedState) confirm Trump made this exact statement at the May 27, 2026 Cabinet meeting. However, the substantive claim—that anti-fraud efforts alone could balance the federal budget—is contradicted by fiscal experts: the 2025 deficit was $1.8 trillion while even generous fraud estimates (GAO's roughly $200-300 billion) fall far short, and commentators across the political spectrum called the claim 'wildly false' or acknowledged it 'won't balance the budget.'

claim: ES&S voting machine in Saluda precinct in Greenville County flips a vote
justification: Mark Lynch did post this exact claim and an accompanying video on X, which multiple news outlets reported on, confirming he made the statement. However, no independent authority verified that the machine actually flipped the vote as claimed; one outlet explicitly noted it 'was unable to validate the video's source supporting alleged corruption,' and no election commission statement or investigation confirming a malfunction was found.

claim: Beauty in Black woman seen in the stadium during the FIFA World Cup.
justification: Independent fact-checking by CyberPeace Research Wing found the 'Beauty in Black' video shared by Bal Mukund Joshi to be AI-generated, originating from a virtual influencer Instagram account, not a real woman filmed in a World Cup stadium. Multiple AI-detection tools (Hive Moderation at 100%, Vera AI at 92%) confirmed synthetic origin, and the footage does not depict any real FIFA World Cup 2026 incident.

claim: Singer-rapper Jelly Roll filed for divorce from his wife, Bunnie Xo, in 2026.
justification: Multiple independent, reputable outlets (TMZ, NBC News, Fox News, ABC News, Billboard, Rolling Stone) confirm via Tennessee court records that Jelly Roll filed for divorce from Bunnie Xo on May 18, 2026, with the news becoming public around June 15-16, 2026. The divorce was later finalized in July 2026.

claim: U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., "confirmed" during a June 2026 congressional speech that Israel attacked the USS Liberty, an American naval ship, with napalm.
justification: Multiple independent news outlets (Al Jazeera, Military.com, Daily Caller, Haaretz, JTA) confirm that Rep. Thomas Massie gave a House floor speech in June 2026 (specifically June 8) in which he stated that Israeli jets dropped napalm on the USS Liberty, including on its bridge. This detail about napalm use is corroborated as part of the historical record of the attack, not just Massie's personal claim.

claim: Rodrigo Duterte is going home after his interim release request was approved by the ICC.
justification: Extensive ICC and news records show Duterte's interim release requests have been repeatedly and consistently rejected by both the Pre-Trial Chamber and Appeals Chamber from September 2025 through April 2026, with Duterte still in detention as his trial was scheduled for November 2026. The ICC has never granted interim release to a crimes against humanity suspect, and no credible source reports any approval of his release around the June 2026 date cited in the claim.

claim: In June 2026, the U.S. Postal Service proposed a rule in which it would stop delivering mail ballots for states that do not give the federal government voter lists.
justification: Multiple independent news outlets (ABC News, CNN, Fox News, PBS, Time) confirm that in June 2026 USPS proposed a rule, stemming from Trump's March 2026 executive order, under which Postmaster General David Steiner testified to the Senate that USPS would not deliver mail ballots for states that refused to hand over their voter lists to the federal government. Steiner's direct quote 'Under our proposed regulation, no' and 'We would tell the state that we need the manifest' confirms the central assertion.

claim: Shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump authorized more than $14 million to repaint the bottom of Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool "American flag blue" in 2026, the paint began to peel off.
justification: Multiple independent news outlets (Washington Post, ABC News, Washington Examiner, WTOP, NPR, CBC) and Wikipedia all confirm that Trump authorized a $13-14+ million renovation to repaint the Reflecting Pool's bottom 'American flag blue,' and that shortly after the pool reopened in early June 2026, the paint began visibly peeling off, documented in photos and video by mid-June.

claim: U.S. President Donald Trump's motorcade drove through the newly painted and sealed Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
justification: Multiple independent, credible news outlets (AP/PBS, ABC7, CNN, NBC, Forbes, New York Post) and a Snopes fact-check all confirm that on May 7, 2026, Trump's motorcade drove across the drained Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool after it had been freshly painted/sealed with a blue polyurea coating as part of a renovation, and before it was refilled with water. Video footage and photographs corroborate the event, including tire marks left in the wet coating.

claim: After their 2026 World Cup games at Los Angeles Stadium, the members of Iran's men's soccer team left a note in the locker room calling for peace and thanking the city for its hospitality.
justification: Numerous independent outlets (ESPN, Reuters via FOX LA, UPI, The Washington Times, The Globe and Mail, Yahoo Sports) and a dedicated fact-check all confirm that after Iran's two World Cup group matches at Los Angeles Stadium (SoFi Stadium), the team left a handwritten note, released by Iran's football federation, thanking Los Angeles for its hospitality and calling for 'peace, respect, and friendship' among nations.

claim: On July 1, 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump said, “Now, as I see my two beautiful sons sitting there, I think I’m going to give one [Medal of Honor] to myself, one to them, and we’ll have a threesome, OK.”
justification: Multiple independent sources (The Nightly, USA Today/AOL, inkl, North Dakota Monitor) confirm Trump made this exact remark on July 1, 2026, at the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library dedication in Medora, North Dakota, with his sons Donald Jr. and Eric seated in the audience. The quote matches verbatim across sources, and video clips of the moment circulated widely.

claim: India’s passport ranking was 76th in 2014 and, under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, it declined to 125th in 2026.
justification: The 76th figure for 2014 is accurate for the Henley Passport Index, but the 125th figure for 2026 comes from a completely different index (Arton Capital's Passport Power Rank), not Henley. On the same Henley Index used for the 2014 baseline, India's 2026 ranking fluctuated between roughly 75th and 81st -- essentially flat or slightly improved, not a decline to 125th. Splicing two different, methodologically incompatible indices creates a false impression of a dramatic decline under Modi.

claim: Wikipedia edits prove Francois Letexier, referee in Argentina-Egypt World Cup match, grew up in an "Orthodox Jewish family".
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (Lead Stories/Yahoo, Euronews, Forward, Jewish Chronicle, Breitbart) traced the Wikipedia edits to a specific editor (Maqaumat) who cited sources that made no mention of Letexier's religion or ethnicity. Wikipedia's own editors removed the claim within hours, noting no reliable sourcing existed for it, and the responsible editor was banned. The claim's spread via X's Grok AI was itself an example of 'citogenesis' where the AI cited the hoax Wikipedia edit as its source, not independent verification.

claim: Russia destroyed Skyfall drone facility shortly after Lindsey Graham visited it.
justification: Fact-checkers (Lead Stories) found no credible media reports, no Russian MoD claim, and no satellite/ground evidence confirming that the specific SkyFall facility Graham toured was destroyed. While Russia did strike drone-production sites in the Kyiv region around that time, Ukrainian authorities have not identified Graham's host facility as one of the sites hit, leaving the central claim unconfirmed either way.

claim: A Large amount of cash recovered from the car of an accused in the Ram Mandir offering theft case.
justification: News reports on the Ram Mandir donation theft case describe cash being recovered from accused persons' possession, residences, and even a hidden bathroom stash, and a car was separately seized as an asset purchased with embezzled funds — but no source indicates cash was found inside a car. The claim appears to conflate two distinct, separately reported recoveries into an inaccurate composite claim.

claim: After the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham, U.S. President Donald Trump said in a July 2026 interview with Newsmax that “a certain part of [Graham's] body literally blew up."
justification: Multiple independent outlets (AOL, Yahoo, Wonderwall) confirm Trump made this exact statement during a July 14, 2026 Newsmax interview with Greg Kelly, discussing Sen. Lindsey Graham's death from an aortic dissection. Graham did die suddenly on July 11, 2026, and Trump's quote 'a certain part of his body literally blew up' is directly corroborated across sources, some including video/transcript excerpts.

claim: Antonio Trillanes IV filed a disbarment complaint against the 16 lawyers of Sara Duterte during her impeachment trial.
justification: VERA Files, a reputable Philippine fact-checking organization, explicitly investigated and debunked this exact claim, stating the graphic alleging Trillanes filed a disbarment complaint against Sara Duterte's 16-member defense team is 'not true.' Contemporary reporting on Trillanes's activities during the impeachment trial (October 2026) shows he was focused on withdrawing as a prosecution witness and publicly presenting financial allegations against the Duterte family, with no mention of any disbarment complaint against the defense lawyers.

claim: In July 2026, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced testosterone screening for U.S. troops, along with replacement therapy.
justification: Numerous independent major outlets (AP/PBS, CNN, NBC News, CBS News, The Hill, Al Jazeera, ABC News, Washington Post) consistently reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced on July 15-16, 2026 a new annual testosterone screening program for troops 30 and older, with voluntary testosterone replacement therapy for those recommended for treatment. This matches the claim precisely in substance and timing.

claim: "Teenage males today have less sperm than the average 65-year-old American man.”
justification: Kennedy did make this exact statement on his podcast, but it contradicts well-established medical science. Multiple experts and fact-checkers confirmed that sperm count and testosterone decline with age, meaning a 65-year-old man would be expected to have lower sperm count/testosterone than a healthy teenager, not higher. No reliable data exists comparing teen sperm counts directly to 65-year-olds' as Kennedy claimed; he appears to have conflated a historical decline (comparing today's young men to men decades ago) with an age-based comparison that inverts actual biology.

claim: A Tennessee woman spent six months in jail after an artificial intelligence tool misidentified her as a North Dakota bank fraud suspect.
justification: Extensive independent reporting from at least ten different news outlets (local TN/ND stations, ABC News, Fox News, InForum/WDAY) consistently confirms that Angela Lipps, a Tennessee grandmother, was jailed for nearly six months (July 2025 to December 24, 2025) after AI facial recognition software misidentified her as a suspect in a North Dakota bank fraud case. Court documents, her federal lawsuit, and even statements from Fargo police officials corroborate the core facts, including the AI match, lack of corroborating investigation, and eventual dismissal of charges after bank records proved she was in Tennessee.

claim: Claire Castro criticized Ivana Alawi for helping.
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (Rappler, VERA Files) confirm the quote attributed to Claire Castro criticizing Ivana Alawi was fabricated, with no official transcript, press release, or recording supporting it. Castro herself publicly refuted the viral quote card as fake.

claim: The YouTube channel of the Miami Heat posted a link to a July 27, 2026, news conference announcing the signing of basketball superstar LeBron James.
justification: While the Heat's YouTube channel did briefly post a link to a video titled 'LeBron James Introductory Press Conference' dated July 27, 2026, the team immediately clarified this was a mistaken, premature post with 'no validity' — not an actual announcement of a signing. In fact, LeBron James never signed with the Heat at all; he ultimately signed with the Philadelphia 76ers around July 24-26, 2026. The claim misrepresents an accidental, disavowed placeholder video as a genuine announcement of a signing that never occurred.

claim: The government spends P70 million per day in holding Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial.
justification: A dedicated fact-check by Philstar found no official record supports the P70 million per day figure. Senate President Gatchalian stated the Senate incurs no additional expenses from the trial since it's treated like a regular plenary session, with prosecution and defense covering their own costs; the closest real figure is the Senate's general daily operating cost of about P25 million (which exists regardless of the trial) and other officials cited budgets of under P1 million to P27 million total, not P70 million per day.

claim: The peptide tesamorelin is approved to help with muscle mass, weight loss
justification: Tesamorelin's only FDA-approved indication is reduction of excess visceral abdominal fat in HIV-infected adults with lipodystrophy. The FDA label and multiple independent sources explicitly state it 'is not indicated for weight loss management as it has a weight neutral effect,' directly contradicting the weight-loss portion of the claim. While trials showed a secondary increase in lean body mass, this is not an approved indication for 'muscle mass' and the drug is not approved for athletic/body-composition use outside the lipodystrophy context.

claim: "We inherited the worst inflation in the history of America from the Biden administration. And as you know, last week, it was announced that inflation is way down. It’s down more than it’s been in over six years."
justification: The claim rests on two assertions: that Biden-era inflation was the worst in American history, and that inflation is now down more than in six years. The first is demonstrably false—multiple fact-checks confirm inflation in the 1970s-80s (12-15%) and 1946 (18%) far exceeded Biden's 9.1% peak. The second has a narrow factual basis (a one-month 0.4% CPI drop in June 2026 was the largest monthly drop in six years), but this cherry-picks a single data point while annual inflation remained elevated at 3.4-3.5%, higher than when Trump took office, making the overall framing misleading and the central historical claim false.

claim: August 3 procession in Louisville, Kentucky was to bring Mitch McConnell's corpse to the coroner's office
justification: The Louisville Metro Police Department directly and categorically denied the claim, confirming the August 3 procession was for a deceased police officer, not Senator McConnell. The video's own creator retracted the claim as 'inaccurate,' and multiple independent fact-checkers (Lead Stories, PolitiFact-style outlets, Media Bias/Fact Check) rated it false. Subsequent events also confirm McConnell was alive and later returned to the Senate in September 2026, further contradicting the death claim.

claim: Spokane wildfires intentionally set to make room for data centers
justification: Multiple fact-checks (AFP/Yahoo, local news) and official statements from Spokane city officials, the county prosecutor, and Avista directly contradict the claim. Investigators found the primary fire was deliberate arson by a man with no connection to data centers, the other fires were accidental/undetermined, and the blazes are attributed to extreme drought and wind conditions, not a plot to clear land for data centers. A map purportedly proving the link was also found to be falsely labeled.

claim: In August 2026, the White House's official Instagram account shared Spider-Man-inspired graphics showing immigrants trapped in webs next to a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent.
justification: Multiple independent sources, including a Snopes fact-check (rated 'True') and numerous news outlets (Deadline, TMZ, Euronews, Yahoo News), confirm the White House's official Instagram account posted a Spider-Man-themed carousel on August 6, 2026, showing immigrants/detainees trapped in webs next to an ICE agent, captioned 'Your friendly neighborhood ICE agents.' The claim's central assertion is directly verified by primary source archiving of the actual Instagram post.

claim: "You have the MMR [measles, mumps, rubella vaccine]. We want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together, there could be a possibility they're quite lethal. And separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal but just very effective."
justification: The quote is accurately attributed to Trump at the August 10, 2026 executive order signing, confirmed by multiple independent outlets (CBS, Yahoo, The Hill, Newsweek). However, the central factual assertion embedded in the quote—that the combined MMR vaccine could be 'lethal' while separate doses would not be—is false and unsupported by evidence. The CDC states there is no scientific evidence of benefit to separating the vaccine, and Trump's own CMS Administrator Dr. Oz publicly stated 'the MMR vaccine is not a lethal vaccine,' directly contradicting the president's claim.

claim: U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., voted against or blocked measures mandating employees receive sick leave in 1993, 2015, 2020 and 2022.
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks confirm McConnell voted against sick-leave-related measures in all four cited years: against the 1993 FMLA (unpaid leave), against a 2015 paid sick leave budget amendment, against a same-day strengthening amendment in 2020 (while also voting for the base bill with temporary paid sick leave) and later blocking its extension, and against a 2022 rail worker paid sick leave resolution. The main nuance is that in 2020 he voted FOR the Families First Coronavirus Response Act itself (which included temporary paid sick leave) while voting against efforts to strengthen/extend it, which fact-checkers describe as needing clarification but not undermining the overall claim.

claim: In August 2026, the Trump administration paid German energy company RWE $1.2 billion to stop building wind farms.
justification: Multiple independent, credible sources (BBC, NYT, Washington Post, TechCrunch, Fortune, Mother Jones, Reuters-sourced reports) confirm that in early August 2026 the Trump administration's Department of the Interior agreed to pay German energy company RWE approximately $1.22 billion in exchange for RWE relinquishing its offshore wind leases off New York, California, and Louisiana. RWE itself confirmed the settlement amount and terms in its own statement.

claim: The World Bank classifies Australia as a third-world country.
justification: The World Bank does not use the term 'third world' at all in its classification system, and it explicitly classifies Australia as a high-income economy, a status it has held since 1987. A World Bank spokesperson directly denied the claim to AFP, confirming no such 'third world' classification exists in the Bank's framework.

claim: Due to the increasing population and a lack of space, houses were built inside the crater of a doormat volcano in Mexico.
justification: A dedicated fact-check of this exact Facebook post by 'The Great India' found the viral image was AI-generated (98-99% probability per two detection tools), and that real-world investigation of the actual Xico crater in Mexico City shows only farming occurs inside the crater while residential areas are located outside/around it, not inside.

claim: A technology issue was proof of fraud in 2026 Wisconsin democratic primary
justification: The technology issue (USB drives containing audit logs instead of results) did spark viral fraud claims on social media, but it was not actual proof of fraud. Independent election security experts who reviewed the released audit logs found no evidence of tampering, vote deletion, or manipulation; the ballot counts matched official results exactly, and both candidates accepted the outcome without alleging fraud.

claim: Kill parasites with wormwood, green black walnut hull and ground cloves
justification: Hulda Clark did promote this exact wormwood/black walnut hull/clove combination as a parasite-killing treatment, and isolated lab studies show some antiparasitic activity for individual compounds like juglone and eugenol. However, the specific claim that this combination effectively kills parasites in humans has never been validated in clinical trials, and the FTC successfully argued Clark's marketers lacked a reasonable basis for claiming it 'kills' parasites, while parasitology experts called her supporting case histories bad science. Presenting the claim without this context creates a misleadingly favorable impression of an unproven, legally contested protocol.

claim: In August 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump said of 10-year-old Nathaniel Rai's ocean rescue, "I don't know if I'd do it. I wouldn't, probably."
justification: Multiple independent news outlets (AP, People, Fox News, Irish Star, The Blast, and a dedicated fact-check) confirm Trump made this exact statement during an Oval Office meeting with Nathaniel Rai and lifeguard Ryder Williams. A fact-check verified the quote against recorded video footage of the event. The only discrepancy is the date—the statement was made on August 17, 2026, not August 19 as the claim specifies, but this minor date error does not change the truth of the central assertion that Trump said this.

claim: The Census Bureau found that over 24,000 Noncitizens voted illegally in the 2020 election meaning Trump won.
justification: While a Census Bureau report did cite a figure of over 24,000 voter records matched to noncitizen immigration records (though experts dispute this proves illegal voting rather than data-matching errors), the central claim that this 'means Trump won' is directly contradicted by the evidence. The report itself shows these numbers are far smaller than Biden's victory margins in every contested state and nationally (Biden won by 7 million votes), and critically the data does not even indicate which candidate the flagged voters supported.

claim: Donald Trump said the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
justification: The specific claim that Trump said the US was in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for 2028 stems from a fabricated Truth Social screenshot. Trump's actual genuine post on August 17-18, 2026 only cited India's voter ID requirements and voter turnout figures to push for the SAVE America Act, with no mention of EVMs or any talks to import Indian voting machines. Multiple fact-checkers and journalists confirmed the viral post was fake.

claim: “This past filing season, 440,000 tipped workers right here in Nevada saved an average of $10,000 on their taxes" because of the "no tax on tips" policy.
justification: Independent fact-checks (FactCheck.org, Nevada Independent, Tax Policy Center via Yahoo Finance, Washington Spectator) found the White House provided no data supporting the $10,000 average savings figure, and that it likely conflates the deduction amount with actual tax savings, which experts estimate average only around $1,800 or less. The 440,000 figure also represents workers theoretically covered by eligible occupations, not the number who actually benefited, as many tipped workers earn too little to owe federal income tax and see no savings at all.

claim: Farmers will receive a special ₹4,000 instalment under the PM-KISAN scheme on the occasion of Raksha Bandhan in August 2026.
justification: India's official government fact-checking body, PIB Fact Check, explicitly debunked this claim on August 20, 2026, stating the viral AI-generated video was fake and that no such ₹4,000 Raksha Bandhan installment was ever announced. Multiple independent news outlets corroborated this, noting PM-KISAN still pays the standard ₹2,000 per installment and the 24th installment date had not even been fixed.

claim: Chris Hipkins is suing TVNZ for defamation.
justification: Independent reporting explicitly identifies the claim that 'Hipkins is suing TVNZ' as a fabricated story spread by a foreign-run (Vietnam/Canada-based) disinformation Facebook page called 'Pozitif Yolculuk' targeting Hipkins ahead of the NZ election. No legitimate news source reports an actual TVNZ defamation lawsuit by Hipkins; extensive contemporaneous coverage of Hipkins and legal matters in 2026 relates to unrelated ex-wife allegations, not a TVNZ suit.

claim: U.S. President Donald Trump bought up to $500,000 in Boeing stock the same day the U.S. Navy awarded the aerospace company with an $880 million contract.
justification: Federal OGE financial disclosures confirm Trump's investment accounts purchased between $250,001 and $500,000 in Boeing stock on June 18, 2026, the exact same day the Navy's contracts office announced an $880 million sole-source award to Boeing for P-8A Poseidon training systems. Multiple independent outlets (Yahoo/Snopes, Moneywise, IBTimes, Yahoo Finance/Barchart) and a formal fact-check all verified this timing using the OGE disclosure and the Defense Department's own contracts announcement page, with Snopes explicitly rating the claim 'True.'

claim: Lake Ontario was named by Indigenous people, not after the Canadian province of Ontario.
justification: Multiple independent sources, including historical cartographic evidence and a dedicated fact-check, confirm that 'Ontario' derives from an Iroquoian/Huron-Wendat word (variously transcribed as Ontarí:io, oniatarí:io, kanadario, or skanadario) meaning roughly 'great/beautiful lake' or 'sparkling/shining water.' The name was applied to the lake by Indigenous peoples and recorded by Europeans as early as 1641, well before the Province of Ontario took its name from the lake upon Confederation in 1867.

claim: Doug Ford posted joke about renaming Lake Michigan as "Lake Epstein"
justification: Fact-checks by AFP and MEAWW found no evidence Doug Ford posted a 'Lake Epstein' image; the screenshot's timestamp and fixed '1,100 views' indicate fabrication, and it does not appear on Ford's verified accounts. The joke actually originated with Canadian radio host Dean Blundell, not Ford, as confirmed by Wikipedia's summary of the naming dispute and other reporting.

claim: A federal judge rule certain AI-generated child sex abuse material is protected by First Amendment.
justification: Multiple independent news outlets (Washington Post, Fox News, AP-syndicated local affiliates, dig.watch, and a dedicated fact-check) confirm that on August 25-26, 2026, Judge John Z. Lee of the 7th Circuit, writing for a three-judge panel, ruled that the First Amendment protects private, in-home possession of AI-generated child sexual abuse material that does not depict a real child, citing Stanley v. Georgia (1969) and Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition (2002). The ruling is real and accurately described, though it is narrower than it may sound - it applies only to private possession, not production or distribution, which remain prosecutable.

claim: In 2016, a woman used sheep to map the Faroe Islands after Google left the islands off of Google Street View.
justification: Extensive independent 2016 reporting (CNN, UPI, CBC, Fast Company, Skift) and later retrospectives confirm that Durita Dahl Andreassen of Visit Faroe Islands created 'Sheep View 360,' strapping 360-degree cameras to sheep specifically because Google Street View had not mapped the Faroe Islands, and this effort led Google to eventually support the islands' inclusion on Street View.

claim: Fox News reported Canada refuses permission to ships crossing the Welland Canal if they list "Lake America" in their documents.
justification: Multiple independent fact-checkers (Lead Stories, AFP, The Canadian Press, MEAWW) confirmed Fox News never published such a report, and Fox News explicitly denied it to AFP. The St. Lawrence Seaway Management Corporation, which actually controls the canal, confirmed operations were normal with no ships blocked. The claim traces back to a satirical Russian-language X account.

claim: During a weather broadcast, meteorologist John Morales said of his ability to predict hurricanes in Florida, "I am not sure I can do that this year because of the cuts, the gutting, the sledgehammer attack on science in general."
justification: The quote itself is verbatim and accurately attributed to John Morales — multiple independent outlets (Newsweek, The New Republic, Miami New Times, Alternet, Marketplace) confirm he said exactly this during a live NBC6 broadcast. However, the claim's date of August 31, 2026 is incorrect; the broadcast actually occurred on June 2, 2025, at the start of that year's hurricane season, not in 2026.

claim: A real Truth Social post by Donald Trump announces the Melania Canal will bypass the Welland canal.
justification: Multiple independent fact-checkers (meaww.com, 10News/Snopes, Yahoo News) confirmed the 'Melania Canal' Truth Social screenshot is fabricated and satirical in origin, not a real Trump post. Telltale signs include a 'Satire' watermark, a misspelled username, and an impossible year ('22026'), and no record of the post exists on Trump's actual Truth Social account.

claim: Visuals showing the floods in Nepal’s Rasuwa area.
justification: While a real, deadly flash flood did hit Nepal's Rasuwa district on 26 August 2026, multiple independent fact-checkers (Nepal Fact Check, BBC Verify, AAP, France24) found that a large volume of social-media 'visuals' claiming to show the Rasuwa floods around this exact date were actually AI-generated, digitally manipulated, or recycled footage from unrelated disasters in other countries. The generic claim as framed matches this well-documented misinformation wave rather than verified genuine footage.

claim: "The reason why we have seen a measles outbreak in certain parts of the country is because of rampant illegal immigration into the United States from the previous administration.”
justification: Multiple fact-checks (PolitiFact, CBS affiliate WEAR, MEAWW) and infectious disease experts found no evidence linking illegal immigration to the measles outbreaks Donalds cited. CDC data show only ~0.6% of 2026 cases came from international visitors, while roughly 93-94% of cases were in unvaccinated people or those with unknown vaccination status, with experts attributing outbreaks primarily to declining U.S. vaccination rates and travel by unvaccinated Americans returning from abroad, not immigration.

claim: In August 2026, Buc-ee's convenience store chain CEO Arch "Beaver" Aplin III said the company was focused on building new stores in "conservative, business-friendly" states.
justification: Multiple independent news outlets (Fox Business, Fast Company, Yahoo, Dallas Express, ClickOrlando, and a dedicated fact-check article) confirm that Buc-ee's CEO Arch 'Beaver' Aplin III made these exact remarks on August 17, 2026 at the Benton, Arkansas store opening, explicitly using the phrase 'conservative, business-friendly' to describe states the company wants to prioritize for expansion. The quote is verified verbatim across sources and the attribution and content match the claim precisely.

claim: Data centers kills bees, cattle
justification: Multiple expert sources and fact-checkers (AFP, CRBC News) confirm Zephyr Zoidis did make these claims about data centers killing bees and causing stillborn calves, but scientists and researchers specifically stated the available evidence does not support claims that data centers' EMFs kill honeybees, cause colony collapse, or cause cattle stillbirths/severe health problems. Investigations often found stray voltage from farm electrical faults, not data center EMFs, was the actual cause of reported animal issues.

claim: Visuals show a massive sacred Shaligram stone discovered after Nepal was hit by floods on August 26, 2026.
justification: Multiple independent fact-checkers (AFP, Tempo, The Quint, BOOM, Fact Crescendo) traced the viral visuals to a 22-foot man-made Shaligram sculpture carved by the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts in Jomsom between April-May 2026, months before the August 26 floods. The Nepal Academy of Fine Arts and local municipality officials both confirmed the sculpture is artificial and pre-dates the disaster, and it is located about 400 km from the actual flood-affected area, which was caused by a glacial collapse near Langtang/Rasuwa.

claim: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said "Under capitalism, man oppresses man, under socialism, it's the other way round"
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (Lead Stories/Yahoo, Daily Caller, MEAWW) found no evidence AOC ever made this statement. Her spokesman explicitly denied it to FactCheck.org, and the quote traces back decades earlier to a Soviet/Polish-era joke and has also been misattributed to economists John Kenneth Galbraith and Russ Roberts.

claim: Former U.S. Army Chief Of Staff Gen. Randy George said "Donald Trump absolutely needs to be hospitalized, I'm seriously concerned about his mental state"
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (Lead Stories, MEAWW, Yahoo News) found no credible evidence that Gen. Randy George ever made this statement. The quote is a recycled hoax that has circulated in several versions since 2025, and the posts attributing it to George also contain factual errors about his position and the circumstances of his departure from the Army.

claim: People in need of livelihood assistance can receive P29,000 from Senator Bong Go by registering online.
justification: Rappler's fact-check specifically debunked this exact claim, finding the post offering P29,000 in livelihood aid under Bong Go's name is fake, with the registration link redirecting to an unrelated job-listing site rather than any genuine assistance program. This matches a broader pattern of confirmed scams (including a separate P29,000 DSWD cash aid hoax) where fraudulent pages impersonate officials or agencies to collect registrations, and both DSWD and Go's office have repeatedly warned that no legitimate assistance program uses such online registration schemes.

claim: A nationwide Facebook ban will begin on September 10, with violators set to face penalties.
justification: Rappler's official fact-check explicitly rated this exact claim as false, finding no government announcement, directive, or credible media report confirming a nationwide Facebook ban or penalties starting September 10, 2026. The viral videos making this claim were flagged as AI-generated. Official Philippine government statements (Malacañang/Palace) confirmed the opposite: Facebook was NOT being banned, as Meta had agreed to cooperate with authorities, resolving the earlier 'last resort' threat.

claim: Bunnings will charge charities and football clubs $150 site fees for holding sausage sizzles.
justification: Reporting from The New Daily identifies this exact claim as originating from a known disinformation Facebook page ('Australia Today'), and Bunnings officially confirmed the claim is false, stating it charges no fee for community sausage sizzles and all funds go to the host group. Bunnings' official information pack for the fundraisers also makes no mention of any site fee.

claim: U.S. President Joe Biden's administration renamed roughly 650 geographic features.
justification: Multiple independent sources (DOI official press releases, NPR, CNN, Fox News) confirm that the Biden administration's Interior Department, under Secretary Deb Haaland, renamed nearly 650 geographic features to remove the derogatory term 'squaw' by September 2022, with a handful of additional sites renamed shortly after. This matches the claim's 'roughly 650' figure precisely.

claim: Turkish police will guard the first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) and arrest violators of election laws.
justification: Multiple independent Philippine news outlets reported that the IEMC, a Comelec-accredited election watchdog, explicitly debunked this exact claim as false, stating foreign police forces (including Turkey's) cannot legally enforce, patrol, or police another country's elections. The claim arose from a misinterpretation of an MILF invitation to the Turkish Embassy to merely 'witness' (not police) the elections, and actual security was provided solely by the PNP (9,821+ personnel) and AFP.

claim: The voter registration website VoteSafe.org was funded by Elon Musk's America PAC and it collects and shares users' personal information.
justification: Multiple independent sources, including a dedicated Snopes fact-check that rated this exact claim 'True,' confirm that VoteSafe.org is funded by Elon Musk's America PAC and that its privacy policy (updated Aug. 29, 2026) permits collection and sharing/selling of users' personal information with business partners and advertising networks like Meta, Google, X, and The Trade Desk. This was corroborated by independent investigative reporting (Judd Legum/Popular Information) and numerous other outlets.

claim: Inmates at a Kansas prison donated over $4,000 to a Kansas school district’s lunch debt in 2026.
justification: Multiple independent news outlets (TODAY.com, WKRC, KWCH/Gray News, Newser) and the facility's own social media confirm that nearly 30 inmates at Norton Correctional Facility in Kansas, through the Reaching Out From Within program, donated $3,810 of their own money which, combined with $457 from Kansas Department of Corrections staff, totaled $4,267 toward Norton Community Schools' lunch debt in August 2026. This exceeds the $4,000 figure cited in the claim.

claim: The Commission on Audit received zero funding under the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos.
justification: News reports confirm COA's overall budget under the Marcos administration was in the billions of pesos (e.g., P16.05 billion proposed for 2027), contradicting a claim of zero total funding. The 'zero funding' reports that do exist refer only to specific line items—COA's capital outlay and its IT/digitization plan (ISSP)—not the agency's funding as a whole, making the broad claim a false generalization.

claim: A post shows Vice President Sara Duterte's police mugshot after she was ordered arrested over her grave threats case.
justification: While an arrest order was indeed issued against Sara Duterte over the grave threats case in September 2026, multiple fact-checks confirm no real mugshot was ever taken — she surrendered voluntarily to the court and submitted her own photos instead, which is why she was spared a mugshot (a point of controversy itself). Fact-checkers identified viral 'mugshot' images as AI-generated fabrications.

claim: A 2026 UN survey of conditions in Gaza proves an earlier UN-backed famine declaration was incorrect.
justification: A real UNICEF-led 2026 nutrition survey did find very low acute malnutrition in Gaza, and this has been used by Israeli officials and some commentators to argue the 2025 IPC famine declaration was wrong. However, leading famine researchers such as Alex de Waal dispute that the new survey invalidates the original findings, noting children can rebound quickly from acute malnutrition and that conditions changed substantially after the October 2025 ceasefire brought a surge of aid. The claim that the survey 'proves' the earlier declaration was incorrect overstates a genuinely contested interpretation, since the time gap and improved conditions mean the new data doesn't necessarily disprove what conditions were a year earlier.

claim: 449,000 noncitizens are registered to vote in California
justification: The 449,000 figure actually comes from a 2016-17 Judicial Council of California report on jurors disqualified due to citizenship status, not registered voters. Courts pull jury pools from DMV and tax-filer lists (which can include noncitizens) in addition to voter rolls, so there is no evidence these disqualified jurors were ever registered voters. Multiple fact-checkers (AFP, PolitiFact, AZCIR) have repeatedly debunked this recurring claim since 2018.

claim: Notification issued by the Union Ministry of Finance to merge nine Public Sector Banks into three.
justification: Multiple independent news outlets (BusinessToday, Organiser, Free Press Journal, Gulf News, Angel One, CreditMitra, Oliveboard) and the Indian government's official PIB Fact Check unit confirm the viral gazette notification claiming nine PSBs would merge into SBI, PNB, and Bank of Baroda was fake and was never issued by the Ministry of Finance. The Department of Financial Services continues to list 12 public sector banks with no official merger notification as of October 2026.

claim: Lawyer Michael Wesley Poa has vacated his post as Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson.
justification: A Rappler fact-check published the same day as this claim (Sept 18, 2026) explicitly debunked the notion that Poa had vacated his spokesperson role, clarifying he only stepped down as OVP spokesperson back in November 2024 and continued serving as Duterte's defense-team spokesperson in the impeachment trial. Subsequent reporting through October 2026 confirms Poa continued actively serving as defense spokesperson, contradicting the claim's implication that he had left this post.

claim: U.S. President Donald Trump's administration is considering a deal that would give a piece of Yosemite National Park to a private developer.
justification: Multiple independent outlets (Washington Post, CNBC, KQED, NOTUS/Washington Sun, ABC7) confirm the Interior Department/National Park Service, under the Trump administration, has for over a year been negotiating a land exchange that would give a small parcel of Yosemite to developer Kingsbarn Realty Capital. The developer's own attorney and the Interior Department confirmed discussions are occurring, though both stress no final decision has been made. The only pushback found was Interior specifically denying Trump's *personal* involvement, not denying the administration-level deal itself.

claim: In September 2026, footwear company Converse published an ad that social media users said evoked Ku Klux Klan and lynching imagery.
justification: Multiple independent, reputable sources (AP via NBC News/ABC News, Bloomberg, Axios, PBS NewsHour, TMZ, WWD) confirm that Converse published a September 2026 ad with K-pop singer Karina that critics said evoked KKK hood and lynching imagery, and Converse publicly apologized, pulled the ad, and acknowledged it 'got this wrong.' Snopes independently fact-checked and rated this exact claim as true.

claim: A real CBC news story linked paying for groceries and white supremacy
justification: Multiple independent fact-checkers (Lead Stories, AFP) found no evidence the article ever existed on CBC's website, in Google News, or Yahoo News archives, and CBC's own spokesperson explicitly confirmed the story was fake, part of a pattern of fabricated headlines falsely attributed to the broadcaster.

claim: U.S. troops fleeing American military bases in the Gulf following Iranian attacks.
justification: Multiple independent outlets (CBS News, NPR, Al Jazeera, CBC, Christian Science Monitor) and a Pentagon Inspector General report corroborate that U.S. troops abandoned or rapidly evacuated Gulf bases—including Camp Buehring in Kuwait and the Fifth Fleet HQ in Bahrain—due to Iranian missile and drone attacks during the 2026 US-Iran war. U.S. officials including the Navy's Chief of Naval Operations and Acting Navy Secretary publicly confirmed severe damage and troop drawdowns, corroborating the central assertion beyond just Iranian claims.

claim: Saudi airstrikes on Houthi positions in Yemens capital, Sanaa.
justification: Multiple independent sources (Al Jazeera, Wikipedia timelines, AA, France24) confirm that Saudi-led coalition airstrikes on Houthi positions across Yemen, including Sanaa, were an active and nearly continuous feature of the conflict throughout September 2026, with specific events documented on dates immediately before and after 20 September. While no single source pinpoints an airstrike precisely dated 20 September 2026, the claim is consistent with the well-documented pattern of near-daily strikes during this period of the renewed Saudi-Houthi conflict.

claim: The number of foreign-born people living in the UK in 2024 was up 143% in a decade.
justification: The 13.1 million figure for 2024 and the ~143-149% increase are real statistics from the Migration Observatory/ONS, but that percentage change spans two decades (2004-2024), not one decade as the claim states. The actual decade-long increase (2011-2021/22 census) was only about 34%, so labeling the 20-year figure as a 'decade' change creates a significantly inflated and misleading impression of recent growth.

claim: Burger King is giving away free meals to people who engage with a Facebook post.
justification: No evidence supports a genuine Burger King promotion requiring engagement with a Facebook post; all verified current BK giveaways use text codes, the Royal Perks app, or receipt surveys instead. Burger King's own official help page explicitly warns customers that fraudulent messages claiming they've won contests or special offers are not from the company, matching the pattern of the claimed Facebook engagement giveaway.

claim: Mike Rogers, the 2026 Republican candidate for a U.S. Senate seat to represent Michigan, has received nearly $4.7 million from donors who appeared in the Epstein files.
justification: The $4.7 million figure is independently verified by both the Detroit Metro Times investigation and Snopes using FEC data, and Snopes rated the exact claim 'Mostly True.' However, the claim omits context that most funds came during Rogers' 2024 campaign (not 2026) and went to a super PAC rather than directly to his campaign, and being named in the files is not evidence of wrongdoing.

claim: Saudi paratrooper landing in Yemens capital, Sanaa.
justification: CNN Arabic's investigation, corroborated by multiple outlets (Albawaba, Daily Yemen), found the viral video was old footage of a US Army Special Operations training exercise in Pasadena, California from June 2026, unrelated to any Saudi military action in Yemen. There is no evidence of an actual Saudi paratrooper landing in Sana'a; the claim stems from decontextualized old footage misrepresented on social media.

claim: Russian fighter jets have reportedly struck Ukrainian airbases amid a large-scale wave of attacks.
justification: A large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine on September 22, 2026 is well documented, involving ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, loitering munitions, and over 200 strike drones hitting industrial, logistics, and port infrastructure. However, no source found specifically confirms that Russian fighter jets struck Ukrainian airbases on that date; the detailed accounts of that day's strikes describe missile and drone attacks on non-airbase targets, and reports of airport strikes found relate to a different date (early September) and involved civilian airports hit by missiles, not fighter jets.

claim: Map showing missing persons cases on Jeju island since 2019.
justification: A fact-check by AFP found that of the 13 missing-person cases depicted on the circulating map (purportedly since 2019), only the 4 cases tied to the actual August 2026 Jeju scandal matched official records; the other 9 cases could not be found in any news reports and were explicitly denied by Jeju provincial police and the coast guard, who said they did not match official records.

claim: A U.S. military strike on an IRGC command center in Tehran.
justification: Multiple independent sources (Fox News, Al Jazeera, Daily Sabah) confirm that U.S. forces did strike and destroy an IRGC command/headquarters facility in or near Tehran during the 2026 Iran war, using B-2 bombers and bunker-buster munitions. However, these documented strikes occurred earlier in the war (roughly February-April 2026), and I could not find a specific new Tehran command-center strike dated to September 22, 2026 itself, as September 2026 combat was concentrated on Strait of Hormuz/southern Iran targets.

claim: Fred Savage The Wonder Years actor die at the age of 50
justification: Fact-checking outlet Lead Stories investigated the exact TikTok post and found it fabricated, with no corresponding Fox News report and no comment confirming death from Savage's agent. Multiple other sources independently confirm Fred Savage is alive as of October 2026, and this is part of a recurring pattern of Fred Savage death hoaxes.

claim: People outside Alberta can vote without verification of residency
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (AFP, Global News, The Canadian Press, Rebel News) found Zelaya's claim to be false. While initial online application forms did not immediately block out-of-province addresses, Elections Alberta confirmed every application undergoes human review and out-of-province addresses are denied, and actual ballot casting requires ID proving Alberta residency. A test case confirmed an application with a non-Alberta address was reviewed and declined.

claim: Vaccines have been intentionally laced with parasite eggs
justification: Robin Goffe's claim that vaccines contain intentionally placed parasite eggs has been directly debunked by public health experts, who note vaccine sterilization and filtration protocols eliminate all living organisms, and that no credible evidence or lab analysis supports the presence of parasites in vaccines. Multiple fact-checking organizations (AFP, PolitiFact, Science Feedback) examining this and similar claims found them unsupported, with CDC-listed vaccine ingredients containing no parasites.

claim: Thirty-five Pennsylvania Republicans voted against a bill that guaranteed daily recess for children in the state.
justification: Snopes fact-checked this exact claim and rated it 'True.' Official Pennsylvania legislative vote records confirm that across the House and Senate votes on House Bill 1505, 30 House Republicans and 5 Senate Republicans voted against the bill, totaling 35 Republicans, and the bill did include the mandatory daily recess provision before being signed into law by Gov. Shapiro.

claim: Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo challenged Vice President Sara Duterte to a debate for the 2028 presidential elections.
justification: A fact-check found that the debate-challenge claim stems from an out-of-context video of Robredo discussing a local hackathon, misrepresented with added text. Robredo has repeatedly and publicly ruled out any 2028 national run, including a presidential bid, and has not challenged Sara Duterte to any debate.

claim: There is real reporting from ABC, CNN and CBS about Fred Durst, Krist Novoselic, and Damon Albarn each criticizing democrats before midterm elections.
justification: A dedicated fact-check (Lead Stories, republished by Yahoo News) examined this exact claim about ABC, CNN, and CBS reporting on Fred Durst, Krist Novoselic, and Damon Albarn criticizing Democrats before the midterms, and found no corresponding reporting existed from any of these outlets or other reliable sources. The claim stems from deceptively edited videos using fake news logos, not genuine reporting.

claim: A Russian missile and drone attack on Ukraine.
justification: Multiple independent sources (Ukrainska Pravda, Kyiv Independent, RBC-Ukraine, Al Jazeera, ISW, and the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission) all confirm that Russia launched a large combined missile and drone attack on Ukraine on the night of September 23-24, 2026, using Zircon, Iskander-M, S-400, and KN-23 missiles along with 282 drones, targeting Kyiv, Odesa and other regions.

claim: Israel's biggest loss is a $30 billion fighter jet, its newest technological aircraft, equipped with three or four engines. At least five fighters were targeted.
justification: The claim describes Israel's newest fighter (clearly referencing the F-35I Adir) as having 'three or four engines,' but the F-35 is a single-engine aircraft, and no fighter jet has 3-4 engines. The $30 billion per-jet cost figure is also wildly inconsistent with actual F-35 unit costs (tens of millions) or even full Israeli procurement deals (~$24 billion for an entire fleet). This matches a long pattern of unverified Iranian state-media claims of multiple F-35 shootdowns that Israel has explicitly denied as 'fake news' and that independent analysts like Janes found no evidence to support.

claim: To celebrate its birthday, Morrisons is giving a free food box to everyone who likes and comments ‘Box’ on a Facebook post.
justification: This claim matches the exact template of a recurring, officially debunked Facebook scam in which fake posts impersonate Morrisons' 'birthday' to solicit likes/comments for free food boxes, which Morrisons has repeatedly and publicly stated it has no affiliation with. No legitimate source confirms Morrisons ran such a promotion on or around 25 September 2026; all available evidence points to this being another iteration of the known hoax used to harvest Facebook engagement and personal data.

claim: The reason for high U.S. gas prices in 2026 wasn't the Iran war but instead California Gov. Gavin Newsom forcing four California refineries to close.
justification: Independent fact-checking (Snopes) and industry sources confirm only two California refineries closed, not four, and refinery executives (Phillips 66, Valero) attributed closures to high costs and low earnings, not a Newsom mandate forcing closure. Energy analysts (GasBuddy, IER) identified the Iran war and Strait of Hormuz disruptions as the primary driver of the 2026 nationwide gas price spike, directly contradicting the claim that Newsom's actions rather than the Iran war caused high prices.

claim: Kenyan governor Wavinya Ndeti facing money laundering charge in the UK
justification: The specific claim of a UK money-laundering charge against Governor Wavinya Ndeti stems from a digitally fabricated Daily Telegraph front page that circulated on social media around August 11, 2026. AFP Fact Check confirmed with the UK Crown Prosecution Service that there is no record of any prosecution against Ndeti or her son, and found no credible British or Kenyan media reports supporting the claim. This is a recycled hoax dating back to similar unsubstantiated allegations from 2024, which Ndeti has repeatedly and consistently denied.

claim: The U.S. was the only opposing nation when the United Nations passed a resolution by a vote of 37-1 to promote women’s equality.
justification: The central numeric fact is accurate: the US was the sole 'no' vote in a 37-1 outcome (with 6 abstentions) at the UN Commission on the Status of Women in March 2026. However, independent fact-checking confirms the claim is misleading in two ways: the action was an 'agreed conclusion,' not a formal UN 'resolution,' and the vote occurred in March 2026, not during the September 2026 session when the claim recirculated, falsely implying it was a recent event.

claim: A Ukrainian attack on the Kuibyshev oil refinery in the Russian city of Samara.
justification: Extensive independent reporting from Ukraine's General Staff, Special Operations Forces, Russian opposition outlet ASTRA, Samara's governor, and numerous international news organizations (Kyiv Independent, Meduza, Moscow Times, Reuters via Kyiv Post) all confirm a Ukrainian drone attack struck the Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara overnight on September 21-22, 2026, causing a large fire. This is consistent with and close in time to the September 27, 2026 claim date.

claim: Recent Attacks on Oil Facilities in Yanbu.
justification: Multiple independent sources (Reuters, Al Jazeera, oilprice.com, Maritime Executive, SAFETY4SEA, L'Orient Today) confirm a sustained pattern of attacks on Yanbu oil facilities throughout September 2026, including strikes on the YASREF refinery, the East-West Pipeline feeding Yanbu, and Aramco terminals, with Houthi claims of responsibility and documented operational disruptions (e.g., SAMREF refinery cutting output by half). While some specific strikes lacked immediate Saudi government confirmation of damage, the broader claim of 'recent attacks on oil facilities in Yanbu' as of late September 2026 is well-supported by extensive independent reporting.

claim: An Iranian strike on an ammunition depot at Jordans Al Azraq Air Base.
justification: Extensive reporting documents over 10 Iranian strikes on Al-Azraq (Muwaffaq Salti) Air Base between March and September 2026, consistently describing targets as fighter jet hangars, maintenance facilities, fuel storage tanks, and command centers—never an 'ammunition depot.' Ammunition depot strikes in this conflict are specifically attributed to Jordan's King Faisal Air Base and Kuwaiti bases (Al Adiri camp, Ali Al Salem Airbase), not Al-Azraq, and one source even warns that strikes are sometimes misattributed between King Faisal and Azraq. No source documents any strike event at Al-Azraq around September 27, 2026 specifically.

claim: Greece's Border Force firing live ammunition at a boat full of illegals and pushing them back into Turkish waters.
justification: The claim is based on a viral social media video with no independent news reporting confirming the specific incident, date, or circumstances. While Greek pushbacks into Turkish waters are well-documented by human rights groups, and there is at least one separate confirmed 2024 incident of Greek coast guard firing live ammunition at a migrant boat (killing one person near Symi), no primary source or independent journalism confirms this particular video depicts a genuine, accurately-described single event combining both live fire and an immediate pushback.

claim: Houthis strike Aramco facilities in Yanbu and Riyadh with ballistic missiles and kamikaze drones.
justification: Independent reporting from Reuters, AFP, Al Jazeera, and others confirms the Houthis did launch ballistic missiles and drones toward both Yanbu (explicitly targeting Aramco) and Riyadh in this period, and Saudi coalition forces confirmed intercepting multiple ballistic missiles. The central assertion that a Houthi strike occurred targeting these two locations with these weapons is well supported, though Saudi authorities did not independently confirm damage to the Aramco facilities themselves, meaning the 'success' of the strike rests on Houthi claims.

claim: Major League Baseball approached U.S. President Donald Trump's administration regarding the possibility of hosting a game at a national park, specifically at Grand Teton National Park
justification: Multiple independent news outlets (Washington Post, AP, The Hill, Fox News, Yahoo) confirmed via on-record White House and MLB officials that MLB approached the Trump administration about hosting a game at a national park, and that Grand Teton National Park specifically was scouted by a National Park Service official as a potential site. The White House's own statement corroborates that MLB initiated the inquiry.

claim: The official poverty rate in the U.S. hit an all-time historical low in 2025.
justification: The U.S. Census Bureau's September 2026 report 'Poverty in the United States: 2025' confirms the official poverty rate fell to 10.2% in 2025, the lowest rate recorded since tracking began in 1959, surpassing the prior record low of 10.5% in 2019. This is corroborated by Reuters, CNBC, Fox News, and independent fact-checks. The claim specifically concerns the 'official' poverty rate (not the Supplemental Poverty Measure, which did not hit a record low), and as worded is accurate.

claim: Al Araby TV reported that Hasakah Deputy Governor Ahmad al-Hilali had died in a traffic accident.
justification: Multiple fact-checks (Al Araby TV's own verification team, Verify-Sy, and others) found the claim was based on a fabricated graphic impersonating Al Araby TV's branding; the channel never actually published such a report. Al-Hilali himself confirmed to local media he was alive and well, and SANA shows him continuing his official duties well after the claimed date.

claim: Japan has officially banned Israeli tourists from entering the country.
justification: Multiple independent fact-checking organizations investigating this specific September 2026 claim found no evidence of any official Japanese government ban on Israeli tourists. Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs continued to list Israel among countries eligible for 90-day visa-free entry, and neither the Israeli nor Japanese embassies' official communications mentioned any such ban. The rumor traces back to isolated private hotel incidents (in Nagano and Kyoto) that were explicitly not endorsed by, and in fact warned against by, local Japanese authorities.

claim: Israeli regime ambassador to the UN was kicked out from the General Assembly hall.
justification: The viral claim/footage being circulated around September 29, 2026 actually depicts Gilad Erdan being removed from the UN General Assembly in September 2023, not a 2026 event. Fact-checkers confirmed there is no credible report that current ambassador Danny Danon was expelled from the hall in 2026; he only approached Iran's delegation with a Starlink terminal after Netanyahu's speech, with no ejection by security.

claim: The effects of the Yemeni strikes on the Saudi enemy capital in Riyadh.
justification: Multiple independent news sources (Al Jazeera, France24, AP) and a Wikipedia timeline confirm that Houthi/Yemeni forces conducted missile and drone strikes on Riyadh around late September 2026, with documented effects including explosions, airport disruptions, smoke from fuel storage areas, and school closures starting September 27. While the specific propagandistic framing of Riyadh as the 'Saudi enemy capital' reflects Houthi rhetoric rather than neutral terminology, the core assertion that Yemeni strikes affected Riyadh is well-documented, though the precise September 29 date corresponds to a period of claimed rather than independently verified strikes.

claim: There will be a "two-moon night" on Sept. 29, 2026.
justification: Fact-checkers (Snopes, via the Yahoo/USA Today syndication) explicitly rated this exact claim 'false,' and NASA's own skywatching highlights for September 2026 do not list any 'two-moon' event. The asteroid cited (2025 PN7) is a tiny, faint quasi-moon roughly 60 feet across and millions of miles away—far too small and dim to be seen by the naked eye, binoculars, or even amateur telescopes, so no visible second moon appeared on Sept. 29, 2026.

claim: Joe Biden removed White House press credentials from over 400 journalists
justification: While it's true that roughly 400-442 journalists lost 'hard pass' status under Biden's 2023 policy change, multiple fact-checkers and even the ABC host directly refuted Scalise's framing in real time: those reporters were not banned from the White House, could still obtain day passes, and a federal court ruled the policy 'reasonable and viewpoint neutral.' Scalise's claim equates an administrative credential-renewal policy with outright removal/banning, which misrepresents what actually happened and falsely equates it with Trump's 2026 outlet bans.

claim: A P50-million fine will be imposed on individual Filipinos for improper use of social media, specifically Facebook.
justification: Fact-checkers reviewing the exact same viral claim found it inaccurate: the P50-million fine proposed in Philippine legislation (House Bill 9965, the Children's Social Media Safety Act) targets social media platforms/companies that fail to protect children online, not individual Filipino users. No bill proposes fining ordinary citizens for improper social media use, and a later consolidated version of the bill even lowered the platform fine to P20 million while explicitly containing no penalties for users.

claim: An F-35 aircraft armament depot and preparation facility at Muwaffaq Al-Salti Air Base in Jordan is being precisely targeted by Iranian missiles.
justification: Iran has repeatedly and genuinely launched ballistic missiles aimed at F-35 maintenance/preparation facilities at Muwaffaq Al-Salti Air Base throughout 2026, so the 'targeting' part is accurate. But presenting this as a confirmed, 'precise' successful strike omits that these are unverified IRGC claims consistently disputed by Jordan and CENTCOM, with high interception rates and no independent confirmation of F-35 damage ever achieved.

claim: A recent Houthi attack on the Saudi capital amid the ongoing escalation.
justification: Multiple independent news sources (Al Jazeera, NPR, CNN, France24) confirm that Houthi forces attacked Riyadh with ballistic missiles starting September 19, 2026, and continued repeated attacks on the Saudi capital through early October 2026, consistent with the claim of a recent attack amid an ongoing escalation as of the September 30, 2026 claim date.

claim: The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump is cutting access to student loans for degrees that have low earning potential, including social work.
justification: Multiple independent sources (Yahoo/Finance fact-checks, WPR, TheGrio, New Republic, AEI, industry financial-aid trackers) confirm the Department of Education finalized an 'earnings accountability' rule under OBBBA that will cut federal Direct Loan and Pell Grant eligibility for degree programs, including social work, that fail an earnings test, with implementation beginning 2027-2029. A dedicated fact-check of this precise claim rated it true. The administration disputes the term 'ban' but confirms the substance of the policy.

claim: President Trump admitted in speech "I've done a shitty job as president"
justification: Trump did literally say the words 'I've done a shitty job as president' in a September 29, 2026 speech, so the quote itself is accurate. However, multiple fact-checkers (Lead Stories, Mediaite, MEAWW) confirm this was a conditional joke — he said he'd have done a shitty job ONLY IF the America.gov website turned out to be his single biggest accomplishment — not a genuine admission that he has done a poor job as president, which is the impression the Instagram post and viral clips created by stripping the context.

claim: Flydubai Plane Making a Hard Landing at Tabuk Airport.
justification: Multiple independent sources (Saudi Gazette, Al Jazeera, CNN, Flydubai's own statements, and Ajel) confirm that Flydubai flight FZ1073 made an emergency/hard landing at Tabuk's Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport on September 30, 2026, following a cockpit altercation. One outlet specifically documented rear aircraft damage consistent with a 'hard landing,' and the plane did land safely at Tabuk as described.

claim: A Houthi attack on Yemeni government forces in Lahj province.
justification: Multiple independent sources (Arab News, Yemen Monitor, Yemen Online, Asharq Al-Awsat) consistently report Houthi ballistic missile and ground attacks on Yemeni government forces (Nation Shield Forces, Giants Brigades) in Lahj province around late September and into October 2026, including specific incidents with casualty figures on September 29-30 and ongoing clashes reported October 1-2, 2026.

claim: In September 2026, social media posts accurately reported that Muslims in Texas are ordering business owners to stop selling haram products — products that Islamic religious law prohibits — within 30 days.
justification: Independent fact-checks (Snopes via Yahoo News, Media Bias/Fact Check) rate this claim 'Mostly False.' While a real Houston imam, Qasim ibn Ali Khan, did ask Muslim-owned convenience stores to stop selling haram products within 30 days or face protests, this was a request (not an enforceable order), directed specifically at Muslim business owners rather than businesses generally, and was the action of one individual with no evidence of a coordinated or widespread Muslim movement in Texas as the viral posts implied.

claim: Discrepancies in ballot folding will disqualify AB mail-in ballots
justification: The claim that folding discrepancies will disqualify Alberta (AB) referendum mail-in ballots originated from social media posts dated September 12, 2026, but was directly contradicted by Elections Alberta, which stated all completed ballot packages will be counted regardless of folding method. A former Alberta election commissioner also confirmed folding has no bearing on whether a vote is counted, since ballots are separated from identifying envelopes before counting.
